claim: Spermatozoa of marine invertebrates are attracted to their conspecific female gamete by diffusive molecules called chemoattractants released from the egg investments in a process known as chemotaxis.
source: Spermatozoa of marine invertebrates are attracted to their conspecific female gamete by diffusive molecules, called chemoattractants, released from the egg investments in a process known as chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and references to prior work.

claim: The information from the egg chemoattractant concentration field is decoded into intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) changes that regulate the internal motors that shape the flagellum as it beats.
source: The information from the egg chemoattractant concentration field is decoded into intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) changes that regulate the internal motors that shape the flagellum as it beats.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's theoretical framework and experimental observations linking Ca2+ signaling to flagellar beating.

claim: Receptor density constrains the steepness of the chemoattractant concentration gradient detectable by spermatozoa.
source: By studying sea urchin species-specific differences in sperm chemoattractant-receptor characteristics we show that receptor density constrains the steepness of the chemoattractant concentration gradient detectable by spermatozoa.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical modeling and experimental data comparing different species with varying receptor densities.

claim: Strongylocentrotus purpuratus sperm are chemotactic.
source: Through analyzing different chemoattractant gradient forms, we demonstrate for the first time that Strongylocentrotus purpuratus sperm are chemotactic and this response is consistent with frequency entrainment of two coupled physiological oscillators: i) the stimulus function and ii) the [Ca2+]i changes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, demonstrated through experiments with different gradient configurations.

claim: The chemotactic response of S. purpuratus sperm is consistent with frequency entrainment of two coupled physiological oscillators: the stimulus function and the [Ca2+]i changes.
source: Through analyzing different chemoattractant gradient forms, we demonstrate for the first time that Strongylocentrotus purpuratus sperm are chemotactic and this response is consistent with frequency entrainment of two coupled physiological oscillators: i) the stimulus function and ii) the [Ca2+]i changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical modeling and experimental data showing synchronization between stimulus and Ca2+ oscillations.

claim: The slope of the chemoattractant gradients provides the coupling force between both oscillators, arising as a fundamental requirement for sperm chemotaxis.
source: We demonstrate that the slope of the chemoattractant gradients provides the coupling force between both oscillators, arising as a fundamental requirement for sperm chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a central conclusion of the manuscript, supported by theoretical modeling and experimental validation.

claim: Broadcast spawning organisms release their gametes into open water where they are often subject to extensive dilution that reduces the probability of gamete encounter.
source: Broadcast spawning organisms, such as marine invertebrates, release their gametes into open water, where they are often subject to extensive dilution that reduces the probability of gamete encounter (Lotterhos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lotterhos et al., 2010.

claim: In many marine organisms, female gametes release diffusible molecules that attract homologous spermatozoa.
source: In many marine organisms, female gametes release diffusible molecules that attract homologous spermatozoa (Lillie, 1913; Miller, 1985; Suzuki, 1995), which detect and respond to chemoattractant concentration gradients by swimming toward the gradient source: the egg.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to historical work in the field.

claim: Sperm chemotaxis was first identified in bracken ferns.
source: Although it was in bracken ferns where sperm chemotaxis was first identified (Pfeffer, 1884), sea urchins are currently the best-characterized model system for studying sperm chemotaxis at a molecular level (Alvarez et al., 2012; Cook et al., 1994; Darszon et al., 2008; Strünker et al., 2015; Wood et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pfeffer, 1884.

claim: Sea urchins are currently the best-characterized model system for studying sperm chemotaxis at a molecular level.
source: Although it was in bracken ferns where sperm chemotaxis was first identified (Pfeffer, 1884), sea urchins are currently the best-characterized model system for studying sperm chemotaxis at a molecular level (Alvarez et al., 2012; Cook et al., 1994; Darszon et al., 2008; Strünker et al., 2015; Wood et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent work on sea urchin sperm chemotaxis.

claim: The sea urchin egg is surrounded by an extracellular matrix which contains sperm-activating peptides (SAPs) that modulate sperm motility through altering intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) and other signaling intermediates.
source: The sea urchin egg is surrounded by an extracellular matrix which contains sperm-activating peptides (SAPs) that modulate sperm motility through altering intracellular Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]i) and other signaling intermediates (Darszon et al., 2008; Suzuki, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Darszon et al., 2008 and Suzuki, 1995.

claim: The biochemical signals triggered by SAPs guide the sperm trajectory toward the egg.
source: The biochemical signals triggered by SAPs guide the sperm trajectory toward the egg.
evidence: This is a general statement about the function of SAPs, supported by the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: The decapeptide speract is one of best characterized members of the SAP family due to its powerful stimulating effect on metabolism, permeability and motility in Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and Lytechinus pictus spermatozoa.
source: The decapeptide speract is one of best characterized members of the SAP family due to its powerful stimulating effect on metabolism, permeability and motility in Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and Lytechinus pictus spermatozoa.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the literature.

claim: The binding of speract to its receptor, located in the flagellar plasma membrane, triggers a train of [Ca2+]i increases in immobilized spermatozoa of both S. purpuratus and L. pictus species.
source: The binding of speract to its receptor, located in the flagellar plasma membrane, triggers a train of [Ca2+]i increases in immobilized spermatozoa of both species (Wood et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wood et al., 2003.

claim: The calcium signal triggered by speract was proposed to regulate the activity of dynein motor proteins in the flagellum, and thus potentially modulate the trajectory of free-swimming spermatozoa.
source: This calcium signal was proposed to regulate the activity of dynein motor proteins in the flagellum, and thus potentially modulate the trajectory of free-swimming spermatozoa (Brokaw, 1979; Mizuno et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brokaw, 1979 and Mizuno et al., 2017.

claim: A direct link between [Ca2+]i signaling and sperm motility was established through the use of optochemical techniques to rapidly, and non-turbulently, expose swimming sea urchin spermatozoa to their conspecific attractant in a well-controlled experimental regime.
source: A direct link between [Ca2+]i signaling and sperm motility was established through the use of optochemical techniques to rapidly, and non-turbulently, expose swimming sea urchin spermatozoa to their conspecific attractant in a well-controlled experimental regime (Böhmer et al., 2005; Wood et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Böhmer et al., 2005 and Wood et al., 2005.

claim: The transient [Ca2+]i increases triggered by chemoattractants produce a sequence of turns and straight swimming episodes (the 'turn-and-run' response), where each turning event results from a rapid increase in the [Ca2+]i.
source: Currently, it is well established that the transient [Ca2+]i increases triggered by chemoattractants produce a sequence of turns and straight swimming episodes (the 'turn-and-run' response), where each turning event results from a rapid increase in the [Ca2+]i (Alvarez et al., 2012; Böhmer et al., 2005; Shiba et al., 2008; Wood et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to work establishing the turn-and-run response.

claim: The turn-and-run response seems to be a general requirement for sperm chemotaxis in sea urchins, however it is not sufficient on its own to produce a chemotactic response.
source: The turn-and-run response seems to be a general requirement for sperm chemotaxis in sea urchins, however it is not sufficient on its own to produce a chemotactic response (Guerrero et al., 2010a; Strünker et al., 2015; Wood et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations showing that turn-and-run is necessary but not sufficient for chemotaxis.

claim: Chemotaxis of S. purpuratus sperm in the presence of speract has not yet been demonstrated despite 30 years of research since speract's isolation.
source: In spite of 30 years of research since speract's isolation from S. purpuratus oocytes (Hansbrough and Garbers, 1981; Suzuki, 1995), chemotaxis of S. purpuratus sperm in the presence of this peptide has not yet been demonstrated (Cook et al., 1994; Darszon et al., 2008; Guerrero et al., 2010a; Kaupp, 2012; Miller, 1985; Wood et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the lack of observed chemotaxis in S. purpuratus.

claim: Only L. pictus spermatozoa exhibit chemotaxis under conditions where a specific chemoattractant concentration gradient is generated by photoactivating caged speract, while S. purpuratus spermatozoa do not.
source: A comparison between individual L. pictus and S. purpuratus sperm responses to a specific chemoattractant concentration gradient generated by photoactivating caged speract (CS) revealed that only L. pictus spermatozoa exhibit chemotaxis under these conditions (Guerrero et al., 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guerrero et al., 2010a.

claim: L. pictus spermatozoa experience [Ca2+]i fluctuations and pronounced turns while swimming in descending speract gradients, resulting in spermatozoa reorienting their swimming behavior along the positive chemoattractant concentration gradient.
source: In that study, L. pictus spermatozoa experience [Ca2+]i fluctuations and pronounced turns while swimming in descending speract gradients, that result in spermatozoa reorienting their swimming behavior along the positive chemoattractant concentration gradient.
evidence: This claim describes findings from Guerrero et al., 2010a.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa experience similar trains of [Ca2+]i fluctuations that drive them to relocate, but with no preference toward the center of the chemoattractant gradient.
source: In contrast, S. purpuratus spermatozoa experience similar trains of [Ca2+]i fluctuations that in turn drive them to relocate, but with no preference toward the center of the chemoattractant gradient (Guerrero et al., 2010a).
evidence: This claim describes findings from Guerrero et al., 2010a.

claim: The slope of the chemical concentration gradient works as a determinant factor in chemotaxis of chemotactic amoebas crawling up a gradient of cAMP.
source: Previous studies of chemotactic amoebas crawling up a gradient of cAMP, have shown that the slope of the chemical concentration gradient works as a determinant factor in chemotaxis of this species, where the signal-to-noise relationship of stimulus to the gradient detection mechanism imposes a limit for chemotaxis (Amselem et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amselem et al., 2012.

claim: In marine invertebrates, sperm chemotaxis operates efficiently within a boundary defined by the signal-to-noise ratio of detecting ligands within a chemoattractant concentration gradient.
source: In addition, recent theoretical studies by Kromer and colleagues have shown that, in marine invertebrates, sperm chemotaxis operates efficiently within a boundary defined by the signal-to-noise ratio of detecting ligands within a chemoattractant concentration gradient (Kromer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kromer et al., 2018.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa only experience chemotaxis when exposed to much steeper speract concentration gradients than those previously employed by Guerrero et al. (2010a).
source: In this study, we identify the boundaries for detecting chemotactic signals of S. purpuratus spermatozoa, and show that sperm chemotaxis arises only when sperm are exposed to much steeper speract concentration gradients than those previously employed by Guerrero et al. (2010a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The quantity πa/s is the number of receptors that allows half maximal binding rate for any concentration of chemoattractant, denoted as N1/2.
source: The quantity πa/s is the number of receptors that allows half maximal binding rate for any concentration of chemoattractant, which is hereafter denoted as N1/2 (see 1.1. On the estimate of maximal chemoattractant absorption in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a definition derived from the theoretical model.

claim: Only S. purpuratus spermatozoa operate in a regime for which the rate of chemoattractant uptake is limited by receptor density, therefore it cannot be considered as a perfect absorber.
source: Our calculations (see Appendix 1, section 1.1. On the estimate of maximal chemoattractant absorption) indicate that only S. purpuratus spermatozoa operate in a regime for which the rate of chemoattractant uptake is limited by receptor density, therefore it cannot be considered as a perfect absorber.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The actual number of speract receptors for S. purpuratus is approximately 2×10^4 per sperm cell which is fewer than the estimate of N1/2 ~ 3×10^4.
source: The actual number of speract receptors for this species is approximately 2×104 per sperm cell which is fewer than the estimate of N1/2 ~ 3×104 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: L. pictus and A. punctulata spermatozoa seem to approximate toward operating as perfect absorbers.
source: In contrast, L. pictus and A. punctulata spermatozoa seem to approximate toward operating as perfect absorbers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There are meaningful species-specific differences in chemoattractant receptor density which could by themselves explain differences in chemotactic behavior.
source: In conclusion, there are meaningful species-specific differences in chemoattractant receptor density which could by themselves explain differences in chemotactic behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical modeling and data analysis.

claim: A functional chemotactic signaling system must remain unresponsive while the cell swims through an isotropic chemoattractant concentration field and must trigger a directional motility response if the cell moves across a concentration gradient.
source: A functional chemotactic signaling system must remain unresponsive while the cell swims through an isotropic chemoattractant concentration field and must trigger a directional motility response if the cell moves across a concentration gradient (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of chemotaxis, supported by the theoretical framework.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio for gradient detection is SNR = vΔt^(3/2)(4πDac−(N/(N + πa/s)))^(1/2)ξ > 1.
source: Noting that the left-hand side of the condition represents the chemotactic signal and the right-hand side is a measurement of the background noise, Equation (2) can be rewritten in terms of signal-to-noise ratio:
evidence: This is a theoretical equation derived from the chemoreception model.

claim: At low concentrations of chemoattractant (below 10^−8 M), stochastic fluctuations begin to mask the signal.
source: However, at low concentrations of chemoattractant (below 10−8 M), keeping all other parameters equal, stochastic fluctuations begin to mask the signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: In the low-concentration regime, steeper chemoattractant gradients (ξ > 10^−3 µm^−1) are dependably detected by spermatozoa, that is SNR > 1.
source: In this low-concentration regime, the steepness of the chemoattractant concentration gradient is determinant for chemoattractant detection. Shallow gradients result in insufficient SNR, while steeper chemoattractant gradients (ξ > 10−3 µm−1) are dependably detected by spermatozoa, that is SNR > 1 (Figure 1d-f).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: A. punctulata spermatozoa are very sensitive to resact (presumably reacting to single molecules) due the high density of resact receptors (~3×10^5 per cell), which allows them to sense this chemoattractant at low picomolar concentrations.
source: Previous reports show that A. punctulata spermatozoa are very sensitive to resact (presumably reacting to single molecules) due the high density of resact receptors (~3×105 per cell), which allows them to sense this chemoattractant at low picomolar concentrations (Kashikar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kashikar et al., 2012.

claim: L. pictus and S. purpuratus spermatozoa bear lower densities of chemoattractants receptors, approximately 6.3×10^4 and 2×10^4 receptors/cell, respectively.
source: In contrast, L. pictus and S. purpuratus spermatozoa bear lower densities of chemoattractants receptors, approximately 6.3×104 and 2×104 receptors/cell, respectively (Nishigaki et al., 2001; Nishigaki and Darszon, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nishigaki et al., 2001 and Nishigaki and Darszon, 2000.

claim: The spermatozoa of A. punctulata are likely more sensitive to resact than those of either L. pictus or S. purpuratus species to the same mean concentration gradients of speract.
source: According to these species-specific differences in chemoattractant receptor densities, Figure 1d–f suggests that the spermatozoa of A. punctulata are likely more sensitive to resact, than those of either L. pictus or S. purpuratus species to the same mean concentration gradients of speract; with the spermatozoa of S. purpuratus being less sensitive than those of L. pictus species to equivalent speract gradients and mean concentrations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa should only respond to the chemoattractants at higher mean speract concentrations and at steeper gradients than those that elicit chemotaxis in L. pictus spermatozoa.
source: Moreover, the constraints on SNR imply that S. purpuratus spermatozoa should only respond to the chemoattractants at higher mean speract concentrations and at steeper gradients than those that elicit chemotaxis in L. pictus spermatozoa (compare Figure 1d and e).
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model, supported by Figure 1d and e.

claim: The scaling factor SF = ξ_purpuratus/ξ_pictus = (v_pictus/v_purpuratus)(Δt_pictus/Δt_purpuratus)^(3/2)(Z_pictus/Z_purpuratus)^(1/2) ~ 3.
source: We compute the ratio of the slopes of the speract concentration gradient experienced by either S. purpuratus or L. pictus spermatozoa, which represents a scaling factor (SF) in the gradient slope, expressed as:
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation based on the chemoreception model.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa may detect chemoattractant gradients in the 10^−9 M regime with sufficient certainty only if the slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradient is greater than 3×10^−3 µm^−1 (i.e. steep concentration gradients).
source: In summary, the chemoreception model suggests that S. purpuratus spermatozoa detect chemoattractant gradients with lower sensitivity than those of L. pictus. It also predicts that S. purpuratus spermatozoa may detect chemoattractant gradients in the 10−9 M regime with sufficient certainty only if the slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradient is greater than 3×10−3 µm−1 (i.e. steep concentration gradients) (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model, supported by Figure 1d.

claim: The experimental setup generates determined speract concentration gradients by focusing a brief (200 ms) flash of UV light along an optical fiber, through the objective, and into a field of swimming S. purpuratus spermatozoa containing caged-speract (CS) at 10 nM in artificial sea water.
source: Our experimental setup is designed to generate determined speract concentration gradients by focusing a brief (200 ms) flash of UV light along an optical fiber, through the objective, and into a field of swimming S. purpuratus spermatozoa containing caged-speract (CS) at 10 nM in artificial sea water (Guerrero et al., 2010a; Tatsu et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The slope of the speract concentration gradient was varied by separately employing four optical fibers of distinct diameters, arranged into five different configurations (f1, f2, f3, f4, f5).
source: To test experimentally whether S. purpuratus spermatozoa undergo chemotaxis, as predicted from the chemoreception model, we varied the slope of the speract concentration gradient by separately employing four optical fibers of distinct diameters, arranged into five different configurations (f1, f2, f3, f4, f5) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes the experimental design used to test the predictions.

claim: Each fiber configuration produces a characteristic pattern of UV illumination within the imaging field.
source: Each configuration produces a characteristic pattern of UV illumination within the imaging field (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The highest concentration of speract released through photo-liberation from CS is generated by the f5 fiber, followed by f4>f3>f2>f1.
source: By examining these UV irradiation patterns, the highest concentration of speract released through photo-liberation from CS is generated by the f5 fiber, followed by f4>f3>f2>f1 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The steepest UV irradiation gradients are those generated by the f2, f3 and f5 fibers.
source: The steepest UV irradiation gradients are those generated by the f2, f3 and f5 fibers (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Irrespective of the optical fiber used, the photo-activation of caged speract triggers the stereotypical Ca2+-dependent motility responses of S. purpuratus spermatozoa.
source: Irrespective of the optical fiber used, the photo-activation of caged speract triggers the stereotypical Ca2+-dependent motility responses of S. purpuratus spermatozoa (Figure 2d, Video 1, Appendix 1—video 1 and Appendix 1—videos 4, 5 and 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d and associated videos.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa accumulate significantly toward the center of the speract gradients generated by the f2- and f3-fibers.
source: In summary, S. purpuratus spermatozoa accumulate significantly toward the center of the speract gradients generated by the f2- and f3-fibers (Figure 3b), which provide UV light profiles with steeper slopes compared to the f1 and f4 fibers (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b and Figure 2b.

claim: The use of fibers f4 and f5 uncages higher concentrations of speract (by providing higher UV energies than other fibers), yet they do not trigger the maximum accumulation of S. purpuratus spermatozoa at the center of the chemoattractant field.
source: Notably, the use of fibers f4 and f5 uncages higher concentrations of speract (by providing higher UV energies than other fibers) (Figure 2a and Supplementary file 2), yet they do not trigger the maximum accumulation of S. purpuratus spermatozoa at the center of the chemoattractant field.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The speract fields created by fibers f2, f3 and f5 produce significantly positive CI values compared to other conditions (f1, f4 and negative controls), confirming that steeper speract concentration gradients trigger chemotactic responses in S. purpuratus spermatozoa.
source: The speract fields created by fibers f2, f3 and f5 produce significantly positive CI values compared to other conditions (f1, f4 and negative controls), confirming that steeper speract concentration gradients trigger chemotactic responses in S. purpuratus spermatozoa.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The lack of chemotactic responses in S. purpuratus spermatozoa observed by Guerrero et al. (2010a) was reproduced through stimulation with f4, zero Ca2+, or High K+ experimental regimes.
source: Again, the lack of chemotactic responses in S. purpuratus spermatozoa observed by Guerrero et al. (2010a), was reproduced through stimulation with f4, zero Ca2+, or High K+ experimental regimes (a scrutiny of non-chemotactic cells is presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and section 2.7. Sperm swimming behavior in different chemoattractant gradients in Appendix 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and discussed in the Appendix.

claim: The percentage of S. purpuratus spermatozoa experiencing relocation increases monotonically with the SNR.
source: In agreement with these results, we found that the percentage of S. purpuratus spermatozoa experiencing relocation increases monotonically with the SNR (Figure 4f), within the noise limits of 0.1 < SNR < 0.8, which is also in agreement with the findings of sperm chemotaxis operating optimally in the presence of noise (Amselem et al., 2012; Kromer et al., 2018; Lazova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4f and supported by citations.

claim: The relative slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradients required for S. purpuratus chemotaxis is at least three times greater than that experienced when exposed to the f4-generated speract gradient.
source: This relative slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradients is at least three times greater than that experienced when exposed to the f4-generated speract gradient (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b.

claim: L. pictus spermatozoa undergo chemotaxis when exposed to the f4 speract gradient, which is 2–3 times smaller than that required by S. purpuratus.
source: In addition, L. pictus spermatozoa undergo chemotaxis when exposed to the f4 speract gradient, which is 2–3 times smaller than that required by S. purpuratus (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b.

claim: These findings support the predicted scaling rule for the detection of the speract concentration gradient between L. pictus and S. purpuratus spermatozoa.
source: These findings support the predicted scaling rule for the detection of the speract concentration gradient between L. pictus and S. purpuratus spermatozoa (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b and c.

claim: The slope of the speract concentration gradient regulates the coupling between the stimulus function and the internal Ca2+ oscillator triggered by speract.
source: To test the hypothesis that the slope of the speract concentration gradient regulates the coupling between the stimulus function and the internal Ca2+ oscillator triggered by speract, we made use of a generic model for coupled phase oscillators (Pikovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This hypothesis is tested using a coupled oscillator model.

claim: There is a minimum coupling strength necessary for the two oscillators to synchronize (γ_min = Δω/2).
source: There are two immediate predictions from the Adler model: first, there is a minimum coupling strength necessary for the two oscillators to synchronize (γmin = Δω/2).
evidence: This is a prediction from the Adler model for coupled oscillators.

claim: Within the synchronous region (i.e. γ > γ_min), the phase difference between the oscillators is constant and follows the relation ɸ_sync = arcsin(Δω/2γ).
source: second, and within the synchronous region (i.e. γ > γmin), the phase difference between the oscillators is constant and does not take any arbitrary value, but rather follows a simple relation to the coupling strength (ɸsync = arcsin(Δω/2γ)).
evidence: This is a prediction from the Adler model for coupled oscillators.

claim: For cells for which synchronization occurs, the measured phase difference is constrained by the predicted functional form of ɸ_sync = ɸ_sync(Δω, γ).
source: Moreover, and for cells for which synchronization occurs, the measured phase difference is constrained by the predicted functional form of ɸsync = ɸsync(Δω, γ) as can be verified from the collated data shown in Figure 6e and f within the theoretical estimates (see also Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6e and f and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The excellent agreement of the simple model of coupled phase oscillators with the data points to the slope of the speract concentration gradient as the driving force behind the observed synchronous oscillations and, as a result, for the chemotactic ability of sea urchin spermatozoa.
source: Altogether, the excellent agreement of this simple model of coupled phase oscillators with our data, points to the slope of the speract concentration gradient as the driving force behind the observed synchronous oscillations and, as a result, for the chemotactic ability of sea urchin spermatozoa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between the model and experimental data.

claim: Diffusing molecules bind to receptors as discrete packets arriving randomly over time with statistical fluctuations, imposing a limit on detection.
source: Diffusing molecules bind to receptors as discrete packets arriving randomly over time with statistical fluctuations, imposing a limit on detection.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of molecular detection.

claim: There is a lower detection limit to determine the direction of the chemical gradient, which depends on the swimming speed of the sperm, the sampling time, and the steepness of the slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradient.
source: However, there is a lower detection limit to determine the direction of the chemical gradient, which depends on the swimming speed of the sperm, the sampling time, and as shown in this work, on the steepness of the slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradient.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical and experimental work presented.

claim: For almost three decades, chemotaxis had not been observed for the widely-studied S. purpuratus species under diverse experimental conditions, raising doubts about their chemotactic capabilities in response to the speract concentration gradients.
source: For almost three decades, chemotaxis had not been observed for the widely-studied S. purpuratus species under diverse experimental conditions, raising doubts about their chemotactic capabilities in response to the speract concentration gradients (Cook et al., 1994; reviewed in Guerrero et al. (2010a); Guerrero et al. (2010b); Solzin et al. (2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting the lack of observed chemotaxis.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa can undergo chemotaxis, but only if the speract concentration gradients are sufficiently steep, as predicted by the chemoreception model.
source: We showed that S. purpuratus spermatozoa can undergo chemotaxis, but only if the speract concentration gradients are sufficiently steep, as predicted by the chemoreception model (i.e. speract gradients that are at in the region of three times steeper than the speract concentration gradient that drives chemotaxis in L. pictus spermatozoa).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The shallower speract gradients previously tested are unable to generate any chemotactic response in S. purpuratus spermatozoa, despite inducing characteristic 'turn and run' motility responses.
source: This confirms and explains why the shallower speract gradients previously tested are unable to generate any chemotactic response in S. purpuratus spermatozoa (Guerrero et al., 2010a), despite inducing characteristic 'turn and run' motility responses.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous work by Guerrero et al., 2010a.

claim: The guiding chemical gradient must have a minimum steepness to elicit sperm chemotaxis, where the signal-to-noise relationship (SNR) of stimulus to the gradient detection mechanism imposes a limit for the chemotactic efficiency.
source: These findings indicate that the guiding chemical gradient must have a minimum steepness to elicit sperm chemotaxis, where the signal-to-noise relationship (SNR) of stimulus to the gradient detection mechanism imposes a limit for the chemotactic efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental and theoretical work.

claim: SNR can be tuned by the steepness of the chemical gradient, where higher SNR's are reached at steeper gradients, hence increasing the probabilities of locating the source of the gradient.
source: We showed that SNR can be tuned by the steepness of the chemical gradient, where higher SNR's are reached at steeper gradients, hence increasing the probabilities of locating the source of the gradient.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The large majority of marine spermatozoa characterized to date, together with many motile microorganisms, explore their environment via helical swimming paths, whereupon encountering a surface these helices collapse to circular trajectories.
source: The large majority of marine spermatozoa characterized to date, together with many motile microorganisms, explore their environment via helical swimming paths, whereupon encountering a surface these helices collapse to circular trajectories.
evidence: This is a well-known characteristic of sperm swimming behavior.

claim: The intrinsic periodicity of swimming behavior commonly results in the periodic sampling of the cell chemical environment with direct implications for their ability to accurately perform chemotaxis.
source: The intrinsic periodicity of either swimming behavior commonly results in the periodic sampling of the cell chemical environment with direct implications for their ability to accurately perform chemotaxis.
evidence: This is an inference from the swimming behavior and its implications for chemotaxis.

claim: The periodic sampling of chemoattractants by the sperm flagellum continuously feeds back to the signaling pathway governing the intracellular Ca2+ oscillator, hence providing a potential coupling mechanism for sperm chemotaxis.
source: The periodic sampling of chemoattractants by the sperm flagellum continuously feeds back to the signaling pathway governing the intracellular Ca2+ oscillator, hence providing a potential coupling mechanism for sperm chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the experimental observations.

claim: Indirect evidence for the existence of a feedback loop operating between the stimulus function and the Ca2+ oscillator triggered by chemoattractants has been found in L. pictus, A. punctulata and Ciona intestinalis (ascidian) species, whose spermatozoa show robust chemotactic responses toward their conspecific chemoattractants.
source: Indirect evidence for the existence of a feedback loop operating between the stimulus function and the Ca2+ oscillator triggered by chemoattractants has been found in L. pictus, A. punctulata and Ciona intestinalis (ascidian) species, whose spermatozoa show robust chemotactic responses toward their conspecific chemoattractants (Böhmer et al., 2005; Guerrero et al., 2010a; Jikeli et al., 2015; Shiba et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The steepness of the slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradient is a major determinant for sperm chemotaxis in S. purpuratus and might be an uncovered feature of sperm chemotaxis in general.
source: To investigate further the molecular mechanism involved in sperm chemotaxis, we measured both the stimulus function and the triggered [Ca2+]i oscillations for up to one thousand S. purpuratus spermatozoa exposed to five distinctly-shaped speract concentration gradients. We demonstrate that the steepness of the slope of the chemoattractant concentration gradient is a major determinant for sperm chemotaxis in S. purpuratus and might be an uncovered feature of sperm chemotaxis in general.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: A steep slope of the speract concentration gradient entrains the frequencies of the stimulus function and the internal Ca2+ oscillator triggered by the periodic sampling of a non-uniform speract concentration field.
source: A steep slope of the speract concentration gradient entrains the frequencies of the stimulus function and the internal Ca2+ oscillator triggered by the periodic sampling of a non-uniform speract concentration field.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data and modeling.

claim: The transition boundary of the coupling term (the slope of the speract concentration gradient) for the two oscillators to synchronize is very close to the boundary where S. purpuratus starts to experience chemotaxis.
source: We assessed the transition boundary of the coupling term (the slope of the speract concentration gradient) for the two oscillators to synchronize and found it to be very close to the boundary where S. purpuratus starts to experience chemotaxis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Within the chemotactic regime, frequency entrainment of the stimulus function and the internal Ca2+ oscillator of S. purpuratus spermatozoa seems to occur almost instantaneously, within the first three oscillatory steps.
source: Our data indicate that within the chemotactic regime, frequency entrainment of the stimulus function and the internal Ca2+ oscillator of S. purpuratus spermatozoa seems to occur almost instantaneously, within the first three oscillatory steps (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A near-instantaneous entrainment would confer obvious evolutionary advantage under the reproductively competitive conditions of synchronized spawning as undertaken by sea urchins.
source: Whether the proximity of the frequencies of both oscillators is sculped by the ecological niche where sperm chemotaxis occurs is an open question, however, a near-instantaneous entrainment would confer obvious evolutionary advantage under the reproductively competitive conditions of synchronized spawning as undertaken by sea urchins.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: The turbulent environment where sea urchins reproduce directly impinges on the dispersion rates of small molecules such as speract, hence, imposing ecological limits that constrain permissive chemoattractant gradient topologies within different hydrodynamic regimes.
source: The turbulent environment where sea urchins reproduce directly impinges on the dispersion rates of small molecules such as speract, hence, imposing ecological limits that constrain permissive chemoattractant gradient topologies within different hydrodynamic regimes.

claim: The correct scale to consider when discussing the small-scale distribution of chemicals in the ocean is the Batchelor scale, l_B = (ηD^2/ζ)^(1/4), where η is kinematic viscosity, D the diffusion coefficient and ζ is the turbulent dissipation rate.
source: The correct scale to consider when discussing the small-scale distribution of chemicals in the ocean is the Batchelor scale, lB = (ηD2/ζ)1/4, where η is kinematic viscosity, D the diffusion coefficient and ζ is the turbulent dissipation rate (Aref et al., 2017; Batchelor et al., 1959).
evidence: This is a well-established concept in fluid dynamics, supported by citations.

claim: Turbulence stirs dissolved chemicals in the ocean, stretching and folding them into sheets and filaments at spatial dimensions down to the Batchelor scale: below l_B molecular diffusion dominates and chemical gradients are smoothened out.
source: Turbulence stirs dissolved chemicals in the ocean, stretching and folding them into sheets and filaments at spatial dimensions down to the Batchelor scale: below lB molecular diffusion dominates and chemical gradients are smoothened out.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in fluid dynamics.

claim: S. purpuratus is primarily found in the low intertidal zone in a habitat with strong wave action and areas with shaking aerated water.
source: S. purpuratus is primarily found in the low intertidal zone. The purple sea urchin lives in a habitat with strong wave action and areas with shaking aerated water.
evidence: This is a description of the ecological habitat of S. purpuratus.

claim: The more energetic zones inhabited by S. purpuratus, including tidal channels and breaking waves, generate relatively high levels of turbulence (ζ ~10^−4 m^2s^−3) which lead to somewhat small values of l_B and, hence, to steep gradients (i.e. 1/l_B).
source: These more energetic zones, including tidal channels and breaking waves, generate relatively high levels of turbulence (ζ ~10−4 m2s−3) which lead to somewhat small values of lB and, hence, to steep gradients (i.e. 1/lB).

claim: L. pictus is mostly found at the edge of or inside kelp beds, well below the low tide mark where the levels of turbulence are much more moderate (ζ ~10^−6 m^2s^−3).
source: L. pictus, on the contrary, is mostly found at the edge of or inside kelp beds, well below the low tide mark where the levels of turbulence are much more moderate (ζ ~10−6 m2s−3) (Jimenez, 1997; Thorpe, 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the ecological habitat of L. pictus, supported by citations.

claim: The ratio of l_B for the different habitats scales as l_B_purpuratus/l_B_pictus ~ (ζ_pictus/ζ_purpuratus)^(1/4) ~ 3, which fits considerably well with the relative sensitivity to speract of the two species.

claim: S. purpuratus spermatozoa experience chemotaxis toward steeper speract gradients than those that guide L. pictus spermatozoa, which is compatible with the distinct chemoattractant gradients they might naturally encounter during their journey in search of an egg.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that S. purpuratus spermatozoa experience chemotaxis toward steeper speract gradients than those that guide L. pictus spermatozoa, which is also compatible with the distinct chemoattractant gradients they might naturally encounter during their journey in search of an egg.
evidence: This is a conclusion that connects the experimental findings to the ecological context.
